key_insight: The paper introduces a practical auditing framework that reveals which clinical ethical principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice) language-model ‘AI doctors’ prioritize, and shows that models vary and often fail to reflect the pluralism expected in patient-centered care.
problem_solved: Provides a systematic way to evaluate and quantify the ethical values that LLMs express in clinical advice, addressing the lack of tools to detect when models impose single ethical stances or mishandle conflicts among legitimate principles.
method: Construct diverse clinical vignettes that surface conflicts among core clinical ethics principles (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice).
Query multiple LLMs with controlled prompts, annotate outputs for which ethical principles they invoke or prioritize, and measure consistency and sensitivity to case framing.
Aggregate results into quantitative metrics and visualizations that characterize model-level pluralism, dominance of specific principles, and inter-model variation.
impact: Enables AI/ML practitioners to detect ethical biases in clinical LLMs, guide safer model design and prompt engineering, and inform policy and deployment decisions to better support patient-centered, pluralistic medical reasoning.
visual_elements: Audit pipeline flowchart: vignette → model queries → annotation → metrics/visualization
Radar or stacked-bar charts comparing the proportion each model invokes autonomy/beneficence/nonmaleficence/justice across cases
Heatmap (cases × models) showing which principle dominates each response and consistency scores
Annotated sample dialogue illustrating a trade-off between principles and how different models resolve it
paper_title: What Does the AI Doctor Value? Auditing Pluralism in the Clinical Ethics of Language Models
paper_authors: Payal Chandak, Victoria Alkin, David Wu, Maya Dagan, Taposh Dutta Roy
